task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of March 20, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: CellForge Biosciences received FDA approval in January 2025 for Axogene, a CRISPR-based therapy for Pelham syndrome, a lysosomal storage disorder that causes neurological deterioration beginning in childhood.
The list price for Axogene is $3.1 million per patient; approximately 1,800 patients in the United States are estimated to be eligible.
Leon Dupont, 34, was diagnosed with Pelham syndrome at 22 and is now in a progressive neurological decline; he is eligible for Axogene but his commercial insurer denied coverage in February 2025.
Dupont said: "I found out it exists. I found out it was approved. I found out I can't have it. That sequence is its own kind of cruelty."

CellForge CEO Adrian Walsh said the price reflects a development investment of more than $900 million and the expectation of treating fewer than 200 patients per year: "We cannot price this like a mass-market drug. The math doesn't work."
Dr. Reena Singh, a rare disease specialist at Northgate Children's Hospital, said three of her patients are eligible for Axogene; none have secured coverage as of March 2025.
Dr. Singh said: "Approval is the first door. Insurance is the second. For rare disease therapies at this price point, the second door is harder to open than the first."

CellForge has a patient assistance program that provides free therapy to uninsured or Medicaid patients; the program currently has 14 applications, of which four have been approved and the others are under review.

Walsh said CellForge is pursuing outcomes-based contracts with major insurers, in which partial refunds would be offered if the therapy fails to halt neurological progression at 18 months; two insurers have agreed in principle, four others have not responded.

The Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER), a nonprofit that assesses drug value, found Axogene cost-effective at prices between $1.8 million and $2.6 million but not at $3.1 million under standard threshold criteria.

Walsh said ICER's thresholds do not capture the full value to patients and families of arresting a fatal pediatric disease: "The quality-of-life metrics ICER uses were not built for diseases like this."
Dupont has launched an advocacy campaign with four other Pelham patients; they have met with three congressional staffers and written to their state insurance commissioner.
Dupont said: "I'm thirty-four. I don't have a decade. The system is designed for people who have a decade to fight."
Dr. Singh said the access pattern she sees reflects a structural problem: payers lack frameworks for one-time gene therapies at this scale, so they revert to denial while developing policies.
Medicaid programs in seven states have issued coverage policies for Axogene; 18 states are still developing policies; 25 states have not addressed the therapy.
CellForge has established two certified treatment centers; Dupont lives 340 miles from the nearest one.
Walsh said the company expects that within 18 months, most major payers will have coverage policies in place; he acknowledged this is not helpful to current patients.

A health policy researcher, Dr. Marcus Adem of Clearview Policy Institute, said the Axogene access gap is predictable: every CRISPR therapy approved in the next decade will face the same structural barriers unless payers develop gene therapy-specific coverage frameworks now.
Dupont said he has not given up on getting treatment: "My situation is urgent. But the reason I'm fighting publicly is for the person who gets diagnosed next year, when the system still isn't ready."

Dr. Singh said the approval of Axogene is a genuine medical advance for Pelham syndrome: "The disease couldn't be treated. Now it can. That is real. The access problem is real too. Both things are true."
